name: Bilal Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent a room above a barber's on the high street of an old railway town, and I walk or get the bus to most of my calls. I work for a small family agency run by Mrs Pritchard, who started it in her front room twenty years ago. My first call is Mr Hughes, an old railwayman who tells me the same story about the 1968 snow every morning, and I don't mind. I also see Mrs Begum, and I help her daughter understand the care plan, because I speak a bit of Urdu.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being trusted in someone's home. That means something to me, it's how I was brought up. What wears me out is that I'm still slow, still learning the medication rules, and I've been told off twice for my notes. And money. I send my mum eighty pounds a month since Dad died, so by the end of the month I'm scraping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because some things should be done by people. I'd say it to the lads at the mosque and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means nothing changes, and that's a mixed thing. My job's safe, but I'm still on low pay in a town with one big agency and Mrs Pritchard's little one. I'd still be scraping every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and try to get better at the notes so Mrs Pritchard stops having to check them. I'd look at an apprenticeship, maybe electrical, because a trade's a trade. And I'd keep sending Mum her money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, I suppose. Not happy, not upset. If AI turns out to be hype, I'm still a carer who sends my widowed mum eighty pounds a month and eats beans by the twentieth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You send your mum eighty pounds a month. What would happen if you couldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd struggle. She has her pension and a bit of cleaning work, but the heating bill alone is more than she can do. My brother sends something too, but he's got kids now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. I sometimes ask a chatbot to explain a medicine name in plain words before a call. Mrs Pritchard showed me, actually. She uses it for her invoices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the hands-on work is still ours, and that's something to be proud of. I'd tell younger lads that a trade is worth more than a desk job now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it might help me with my notes, which are my weak spot. But I'd worry about Mrs Pritchard keeping up with the big agencies. If the big ones use AI to cut their prices, a little agency like hers could go under.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the notes app once the others had tried it, because it'd help my weak spot. I'd go for the electrical apprenticeship, because robots come slower to trades. I'd cut my phone bill and gym to save for the course time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit nervous for Mrs Pritchard. Hopeful for me, a little. A small agency built in my boss Mrs Pritchard's front room can't fight a national firm with a computer doing its rotas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to Mrs Pritchard's agency?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She might have to sell to a bigger firm, or use AI herself to keep up. She's sixty-two, and I don't know if she has the energy. I'd offer to help her learn it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still look at the electrical apprenticeship in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, more than ever. Thinking AI takes desk work first, so a trade with your hands looks safer. I'd still keep some care shifts while I trained.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and people aren't ready. I'd say families will have to look after each other more, like we used to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it means I'd be out of care by 2031, and maybe out of a trade too, if robots can wire a house. I'd be thirty-one with no savings and Mum relying on me. That's the bit that keeps me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish whatever apprenticeship I could in the time, maybe a fast one. I'd move back in with Mum to save rent, so we both pay less. I'd ask my brother and the mosque about any work going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. I'd be thirty-one, with no savings and a widowed mum relying on me, when the robots come for both care and wiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots come about 3 years after thinking AI. Does that hit a trade like electrical work too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yeah, a few years later. The robots would come for anything hands-on in 2031. Maybe the old houses are harder, but I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her not to worry and that I'd move back home. She'd be pleased, honestly, she hates me living above the barber's. We'd manage together, like families should.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time, so people should learn a trade or skill now. I'd tell my nephews to look at apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be all right for a few years, but I'd still have to change by thirty-four. Five years is enough to finish an apprenticeship properly. I'd be a qualified electrician by about 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the apprenticeship next year, keep some care shifts, and save what I could. I'd learn AI tools once others showed me, maybe for working out wiring jobs. And I'd keep sending Mum her money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but I can see a way through. Five years is enough for me to go from carer to qualified electrician, if I start the year it's announced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does five years change your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If there were help with apprenticeships, I'd take it. That's not a handout, that's an investment. Benefits I'd only take if there was nothing else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said families should look after each other. Would you want any government help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not much else. I'd want to pay my own way. But training help, yes, because that's for work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time for everyone to plan. I'd tell the lads at the mosque to save and learn a trade, not wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is enough to get a trade and a bit of savings. I'd be forty when robots come, and I'd hope to have my own small business by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep caring for a couple of years, then do the apprenticeship. I'd save steadily and maybe start my own small electrical business. I'd still send Mum money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better, calmer. Ten years is enough time to get a trade, help my mum, and maybe start a small business before the robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you stay in care longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe two or three more years. I like it, and Mrs Pritchard needs people. But I'd want a trade before thirty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your life look like in 2040?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Married, I hope, with a small business and a van. Mum close by. And maybe still visiting Mr Hughes's family, if he's not around by then.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have no time to get a trade and Mum would have nobody. What would help is funded apprenticeships for people like me, and a bit more pay now so I can save. A trade and a family that sticks together will see us through more than any government cheque.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe the language thing. Mrs Begum's daughter needs me to explain the care plan in Urdu. A robot might do that too, I suppose, but it wouldn't know her.

headlineQuote: A trade and a family that sticks together will see us through more than any government cheque.
portrait: Bilal is a **27-year-old** carer who rents a room above a barber's in an old railway town.
He works for **Mrs Pritchard's** small family agency and sends his widowed mum money.
He uses AI **now and then** to explain medicine names before calls.
He sees a **trade** as his way out, and grows alarmed only when AGI comes in two years.
His values are **family**, faith and paying his own way.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd have no time to get a trade and Mum would have nobody.
whatWouldHelp: A bit more **pay now** so he can save.
